newsitem.title: BOSNIA: President says hardliners isolate Bosnian Serbs.
newsitem.headline: President says hardliners isolate Bosnian Serbs.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic on Tuesday accused hardliners grouped round indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic of leading the Serb republic into chaos and international isolation.
With Karadzic and his allies who control the government preparing to oust her from office, Plavsic told a press conference in her northern industrial base of Banja Luka:
"There is no budget in the Bosnian Serb republic. The police are smuggling, the people are in misery and the country is isolated."

Karadzic's ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS), which he heads covertly since international pressure forced him to turn the Bosnian Serb presidency over to Plavsic last year, called a leadership session on Tuesday to discuss her removal.

Relations between Plavsic and the hardliners reached a crisis at the weekend when she tried to dismiss police chief Dragan Kijac as interior minister for refusing the investigate suspect companies run by Karadzic and senior official Momcilo Krajisnik.
Although technically the Bosnian Serb head of state, she was briefly held by Yugoslav and Bosnian Serb police on Sunday when she returned early from a visit to London to deal with the dispute.

Plavsic told reporters that she was systematically excluded from decision-making by hardliners based in Pale and denied the cooperation of key government ministers like Kijac, who are loyal to Karadzic.

The political battle between Serbs pits pragmatists who support some cooperation with international peacemakers against ultra-nationalist diehards opposed to a postwar settlement that has denied Bosnian Serbs the outright independence they fought for.
Under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement engineered by the United States, the Bosnian Serb republic has an uneasy semi-autonomous status in Bosnia alongside a Moslem-Croat federation based in Sarajevo.
Karadzic and other wartime leaders have also clung to lucrative control of the local economy through their dominance of the SDS and the Bosnian Serb police.

Plavsic warned the hardliners that their defiance of the peace agreement could backfire with "the international community taking the simple way out and forcing the Bosnian Serb republic into a unitary Bosnia, which would be a disaster for us.

"We have to go out into the world and cooperate with the world," added Plavsic, who had a hardline nationalist reputation herself during the war but appears to have since perceived a need for poverty-stricken Bosnian Serbs not to completely isolate themselves.
